segments.text: Metabolism is the network of chemical reactions that sustain living organisms, extracting usable energy from nutrients and using it to build the biomolecules described in Chapter 8 — this chapter applies both thermodynamics (Chapter 3) and enzyme-catalysed kinetics (Chapter 4, Chapter 5) to a biological setting.
is the breakdown of larger, complex molecules into smaller ones, generally releasing energy (an exergonic, energy-releasing process, connecting to Chapter 3’s spontaneity criteria).

is the reverse — building larger, complex molecules from smaller ones, generally requiring an energy input. Together, catabolic and anabolic pathways form a cell’s overall metabolism, constantly balancing energy release and energy consumption.

blocks.text: 4. Connections with lipid and amino-acid metabolism

segments.text: Fatty acids (from lipids, Chapter 8) are broken down via beta-oxidation into two-carbon units that feed into the same citric acid cycle used by carbohydrate metabolism, explaining why fats yield considerably more energy per gram than carbohydrates (their carbon is more reduced, so more electrons are available to generate NADH). Amino acids (from protein breakdown) can likewise be converted, after removal of their nitrogen-containing amine group, into intermediates that feed into the same central catabolic pathways — illustrating that carbohydrate, lipid, and amino-acid metabolism are not separate systems but converge on shared central pathways.
Metabolic pathways are controlled primarily through

rather than by simply having reactants always fully react: key regulatory enzymes (often catalysing an early, rate-determining, and effectively irreversible step of a pathway) are activated or inhibited by molecules signalling the cell’s current energy status (such as high ATP levels inhibiting an early glycolytic enzyme) — a feedback mechanism ensuring metabolic output matches the cell’s actual needs rather than proceeding at a fixed, wasteful rate.

items.text: Catabolism releases energy by breaking down molecules; anabolism consumes energy to build them, together forming the cell’s overall metabolic balance.
ATP is the short-term energy currency, and redox coenzymes like NADH shuttle electrons between pathways, ultimately feeding the electron transport chain that produces most cellular ATP.

Glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain form the central pathway of carbohydrate catabolism, with lipid and amino-acid metabolism converging into the same central pathways.
Metabolic pathways are regulated by controlling key enzymes’ activity in response to the cell’s energy status, not simply left to run at a constant rate.
